definitions.definition: Complex exponential smoothing: a forecasting method that combines each past observation $y_t$ and its forecast error $e_t$ into the complex variable $y_t + i e_t$ and forecasts with an exponentially weighted sum of these values, $\hat{y}_t + i\hat{e}_t = (\alpha_0 + i\alpha_1) \sum_{j=1}^{t-1} (1 + i - (\alpha_0 + i\alpha_1))^{j-1} (y_{t-j} + i e_{t-j})$, or recursively $\hat{y}_t + i\hat{e}_t = (\alpha_0 + i\alpha_1)(y_{t-1} + i e_{t-1}) + (1 - \alpha_0 + i - i\alpha_1)(\hat{y}_{t-1} + i\hat{e}_{t-1})$, where $\alpha_0 + i\alpha_1$ is the [[D2:complex smoothing parameter]] and $\hat{e}_t$ carries the information on past forecast errors.

The smoothing parameter of [[D1:CES]], the complex number $\alpha_0 + i\alpha_1$; its real part $\alpha_0$ and imaginary part $\alpha_1$ are the two real parameters estimated, and they set how much of the past observations and of the past forecast errors is carried into the forecast.

The state $c_t$ of the [[D1:CES]] state-space model, which carries information on both its own previous value $c_{t-1}$ and the previous level $l_{t-1}$; it does not correspond to the trend component of exponential smoothing.

[[D1:CES]] extended with a second pair of level and [[D3:nonlinear trend]] states taken at lag $m$, the seasonal period, with its own [[D2:complex smoothing parameter]] $\beta_0 + i\beta_1$: $y_t = l_{0,t-1} + l_{1,t-m} + \varepsilon_t$, $l_{0,t} = l_{0,t-1} - (1 - \alpha_1) c_{0,t-1} + (\alpha_0 - \alpha_1) \varepsilon_t$, $c_{0,t} = l_{0,t-1} + (1 - \alpha_0) c_{0,t-1} + (\alpha_0 + \alpha_1) \varepsilon_t$, $l_{1,t} = l_{1,t-m} - (1 - \beta_1) c_{1,t-m} + (\beta_0 - \beta_1) \varepsilon_t$, $c_{1,t} = l_{1,t-m} + (1 - \beta_0) c_{1,t-m} + (\beta_0 + \beta_1) \varepsilon_t$.

warrants.text: The seasonal model takes the level and nonlinear trend states at lag m instead of carrying a set of seasonal components, so there are no seasonal indices to renormalise. Since non-seasonal CES captures both level and trend series without a choice of trend form, the only choice left is whether to include the lag-m states.

With the imaginary part of the smoothing parameter equal to one CES is the local level model ETS(A,N,N); with it above one the forecasts grow exponentially, as in multiplicative trend models; and the flexibility of its trajectories lets it follow trends that the level and trend classification of exponential smoothing captures only with separate models.

Seasonal CES consists of two CES parts, one at lag 1 and one at lag m, and each part follows one of the CES forecast trajectories, so the seasonal part can grow, decline or oscillate in its own way. The non-seasonal level can become negative while the lagged level stays positive, and the two levels evolve independently, so the seasonal part can change its amplitude and shape without any change in the level of the series.

Non-seasonal CES has an underlying ARMA(2,2) model that is stationary or not depending on its complex smoothing parameter; by analogy, the authors state the same of the SARIMA model underlying seasonal CES. No stationarity condition is derived for seasonal CES.

The count follows from the model equations: each complex smoothing parameter has two real parts, each pair of level and nonlinear trend states needs initial values (m of each for the lag-m pair), and the error variance is estimated.

On the seasonal subset of the M1, M3 and tourism data, CES with its seasonal or non-seasonal form chosen by AICc has lower RMSSE and MASE than every seasonal ETS model, which the authors take to show that the criterion chooses the seasonal form when it is needed. This is an argument from the accuracy results only: no experiment compares the selection by information criteria with other ways of choosing between seasonal and non-seasonal CES.

CES has lower RMSSE than ETS, ARIMA and the Theta method on the M1, M3, tourism and M4 data and lowers the errors of the combination it is included in, which the authors take as evidence that it is robust, while acknowledging that it does not suit every forecasting scenario. Robustness itself is not defined or tested: no experiment examines how the accuracy of CES varies across conditions or departures from its assumptions.

limitations.statement: CES produces very large errors on a few series: on M1 series 47 it fails to identify the trend and its MSIS is 523.034 against 25.590 for ETS(M,N,N), which inflates its mean MSIS, and on the non-seasonal subset it fails on two series.
The parameter restrictions under which seasonal CES is stable are not derived.
The effect of the length of a time series on the accuracy of CES is not analysed.
CES is formulated only with an additive error term; a version with a multiplicative error term is not developed.
The 10 M4 series on which ETS broke down were excluded from the M4 comparison, so the series were selected on the failure of one of the compared methods.

open_questions.question: Whether CES improves the SCUM combination because it captures long-term relations better than ETS, ARIMA and the Theta method, and nonlinear trends without separating level and trend, is not established.
